Welcome from the Editors


19 has moved!

As part of a significant redevelopment project, 19 is now using Open Journal Systems developed by the Public Knowledge Project, both to improve the way it connects with other online resources and to offer readers enhanced access to articles and supporting materials. After a very successful first four years, in which we have seen our reading numbers rapidly grow with each new issue published, we are delighted to move to a format supporting web 2.0 technologies. We hope this will improve the way we handle and preserve our article data, as well as give us room to grow and develop our multimedia content in the future. Most significantly, we continue in our commitment to advance interdisciplinary work in nineteenth-century studies, and to make the high-quality, original scholarship presented at Birkbeck’s Centre for Nineteenth-Century Studies’ regular conferences, symposia and other events available to an international audience of specialists, students, and interested rea ders alike. Our new issue, Transatlanticism: Identities and Exchanges, guest edited by Ella Dzelzainis and Ruth Livesey, is exemplary of this, charting the transformative flow of texts, images and ideas between America and Britain in the long nineteenth century, and featuring contributions from art historians and literary scholars, established academics and postgraduate students.

Exploring the route 19 might take to join web 2.0 has been an intellectual journey of another kind, into the growing world of digital humanities. The redevelopment project began with the aim to aggregate our content with NINES, and to produce XML versions of our articles in order to capture key metadata of article and author details, both to share with other resources and for our own indexing purposes. Whilst our previous format presented PDF articles adequately in the initial stage of 19's life, we were aware that it had no mechanism in place to act as an 'intelligent' archive; there was no indexing or search feature to gather and store data, or process it for readers. In finding a way forward, we have benefited hugely from the expertise of the NINES team in the US, and also the Centre for Computing in the Humanities at King's College, London, who have worked on customizing Open Journal Systems (fittingly for 19, an open source software project) and developing tools to meet the specific publishing needs of the journal. The project has offered us an opportunity to review our editorial policy, and will enhance the quality of the postgraduate technical training we offer to the editorial team at 19. This includes both the opportunity to work closely on an academic electronic publishing system, and also to work in XML technologies. 19 benefits from the fresh insights brought to it by its postgraduate team of editorial assistants, and we look forward to their continuing contributions in shaping and developing the tools, features and ideas of the journal in the future.

19's new format enhances its presentation of multimedia content. Articles are supported by an exciting and abundant range of nineteenth-century visual material, both embedded in articles and specially-curated in image galleries for image-rich articles. These can be accessed by clicking on the 'gallery' link next to articles on the table of contents page, or from each article's individual 'abstract' page. In the image galleries you have the option to play a slideshow of all pictures, or click on individual thumbnails to go to specific images. Clicking on 'view original' in the caption box will bring up the image in higher resolution for closer viewing.

As part of its upgrade process, 19 is also presenting a choice in how to view articles, continuing to provide print-friendly downloadable PDFs, and introducing new HTML versions. From issue 9 onwards, readers can choose which version to select by clicking either the 'PDF' or 'HTML' link next to the article in the 'table of contents' view, or from within the 'abstract' view. (Images aggregate at the bottom of each HTML article). We have showcased a few HTML articles as part of our release, and aim to publish the remaining set by January 2010. Likewise, we aim to upgrade our previous image galleries to match the new format (from issues 5, Visual and Verbal Interactions in Nineteenth-Century Print Culture, and 8, Victorian Theatricalities), and hope to re-publish these by January 2010.

Our article 'abstract' view acts as a hub from which readers can access a variety of features and tools. From this page, you have the option to read items in full, find out more about the author, access other features such as galleries, or add comments. In the right hand navigation bar you will also find a suite of reading tools enabling you to link to a wide range of online databases, archives and other resources for nineteenth-century studies. PDF versions of articles have been designed to open in new windows to allow readers to toggle back to the reading tools via the 'abstract' page. There is also the opportunity for readers to join the debate, either by using the 'comments' feature on each article's 'abstract' page (please note you will need to register as a reader to do this), or by contributing a review essay of up to 2500 words.

19 has a busy and lively intellectual journey ahead. Future commissioned issues include 'Dickens and Science', 'After and Beyond Darwin: Reflections and Discussions on the Darwin Year', and 'London's East End', as well as the continuation of upgrading material from past issues to match the quality of our new format. We encourage you to register as readers so that you can receive alerts for new issues and the addition of new items. We very much hope you enjoy reading our current and past issues in this new site.

Our warm thanks to Heather Tilley, for her expert management of the entire process, to Jim Mussell for his advice and support since the journal's inception, and to Tamara Lopez and Paul Vetch at the Centre for Computing in the Humanities for their technical assistance.

Hilary Fraser and Carolyn Burdett
